analysis.one_liner: Bans airline fees for carry-on bags and requires airlines to publish all their extra fees.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after being referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in April 2010, it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Transportation Department to write a rule barring airlines from charging fees for carry-on bags that fit the airline's own weight, size, and number limits. It would also have required airlines to tell passengers about bag restrictions before they get to the airport, and to publish a public list of every extra fee they charge — for checked bags, food, better seats, buying tickets through an agent, and anything else — updated at least every 90 days.
analysis.who_benefits: Air travelers, especially people flying with just a carry-on bag. They would have kept carry-on bags free and gotten a single, current list of every fee an airline charges, making the real price of a ticket comparable across airlines before booking.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits air carriers from charging any fees for carry-on baggage that fits within the airline's own restrictions on weight, size, or number of bags [S2] [S3].
Requires airlines to make detailed carry-on bag restriction information available to passengers before they arrive at the airport [S2] [S3].

Requires airlines to publish a list of all passenger fees and charges other than airfare — checked bags, meals, preferred seats, ticket agent fees, and other services — available to the public and updated at least every 90 days [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Airlines lose a fee category they had begun charging for — carry-on bag fees — and bear the cost of maintaining and publishing a current fee list. Passengers who don't check bags stop paying a charge; the airline's stated alternative, folding costs into base fares, would raise advertised fares for some travelers.

drawbacks.text: Airlines argue that unbundling fees lets budget carriers advertise very low base fares and lets passengers who travel light pay less; banning one fee category pushes those costs into base fares or other fees instead of eliminating them.

The bill directs a rulemaking but sets no limit on fees it does not ban, so airlines could raise checked-bag or other fees to make up carry-on revenue; the public fee list improves disclosure but does not cap prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The carry-on ban and fee list are modest, consumer-friendly measures: the fee disclosure in particular would have made it far easier to compare the true price of tickets. The main honest objection is that banning one fee by name doesn't lower the total cost of flying — airlines can shift charges elsewhere — so the disclosure piece is the more durable benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in April 2010, read twice, and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Sen. Benjamin Cardin introduced S. 3195 in the Senate on April 12, 2010, on behalf of himself and Sen. Mary Landrieu [S1] [S3].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S5].
Three Democratic senators cosponsored the bill [S4].
The bill received no further action — no committee vote, no floor vote — and died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Airlines that charge carry-on and other ancillary fees kept those revenue streams untouched, and the traveling public never got the fee list or the carry-on protection.

for.name: Sen. Benjamin Cardin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Maryland; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its lead sponsor.

for.name: Sen. Mary Landrieu
for.role: U.S. Senator from Louisiana; original cosponsor

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never reported it out, held no markup, and produced no floor vote.

against.name: U.S. airline industry
against.role: Airlines that charge baggage and other passenger fees
against.what_they_did: Had begun charging for checked and carry-on bags and publicly defended fee-based pricing as letting flyers pay only for what they use.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only Democratic sponsorship (Cardin, Landrieu, and three other Democratic cosponsors), but it never reached a vote, so no one's position is on record beyond sponsorship.

industries.note: Airlines had begun charging fees for checked and carry-on bags, meals, and preferred seats, and this bill would have banned the carry-on fee outright and forced full public disclosure of every other fee. Their interest in keeping unbundled fees runs against travelers' interest in knowing the real price of a ticket.

The bill contemplated routing airline fee information to travel agencies and banning fees for buying tickets through agents, which would have given agents clearer information and protected customers from agent-purchase surcharges.
